b: It was perhaps inevitable that market-driven land use change would come to City Island; the beauty of the place is immediately apparent. Only a quarter-mile causeway separates the small island from the rest of the Bronx, one of the five boroughs of New York City, and yet City Island can seem a world away.

The former United Boat Service Yard at the foot of Carroll Street was the first major maritime property to be converted to residences, becoming in the early-1980s The Boatyard Condominiums. The managing director then of the island’s chamber of commerce told the New York Times, “If the condos do well, then the boatyards and marinas are all going to go.”

Less than 10 years later, the last sail-making loft, Rapsey & Lapthorn, founded in 1915 and a purveyor to America's Cup racing yachts, became The Sailmaker Condominium. All that was left of these two businesses was nominal references to their function before conversion to residential development. Yet, in spite of the loss of major historic waterfront industries, City Island (mostly, see “Know Before You Go”) maintains its small-town, maritime feel.

A half-mile wide and 1.5 miles long, one is never far from the water on City Island. The buildings, even the new construction, are low-rise, providing a sense of sky that is unique to waterfront communities. With only 4,417 residents (2020 Census) and a—“a” as in one—small supermarket, gas station, bank, and hardware store, it is not hard for visitors to picture themselves in a quaint New England fishing village.

The popular seafood restaurants, the principal tourist attraction, contribute to the impression. This is ironic because City Island was not a significant port for fishing vessels. City Island is known for its boat building and repair and if you want to know more about that history, the place to visit is the City Island Nautical Museum.

The museum is located in the former Public School 102 (later, P.S. 17) designed by noted academic architect C.B.J. Snyder and constructed in 1897. The museum contains a main hall gallery primarily composed of two-dimensional material; the Walsh Library with books, ephemera, and other artifacts; the Nautical Room that focuses on the island’s maritime history; a Community Room, which celebrates life on City Island; and the School Room, with an emphasis on local education.

Like many museums in sparsely populated places that have undergone substantial change, the historical museum on City Island is nostalgic, a lovingly handcrafted assemblage of what artifacts became available for exhibition and what might be reproduced (including with a photocopying machine). A larger physical space, and a much larger budget, might have resulted in a more polished presentation, but a good deal of the charm of the museum derives from the manner in which it tells the maritime and social history of City Island.
